_note: WhatsDaf's own English renderings of the Hebrew commentaries on Sefaria (Vilna edition). Keys are <commentary>:<amud><segment>.<comment>. Square brackets are our clarifications. Very long Tosafot are condensed and marked "In brief".
rashi:a1.1: Rabbi Shimon exempts in this one: for they are two [separate] impurities. Regarding each single entry one can say: this path is the pure one. Therefore there is no definite knowledge at the outset, and for impurity of the Temple we require knowledge at the beginning and at the end, with a lapse in between. And the first tanna, who deems him liable, explains his reason below.
gershom:a1.1: [A printer’s note marks that the preceding comments belong to 18b.] And Rabbi Shimon exempts: for there is no definite knowledge there, since he does not know at which entry he was impure.
rashi:a2.1: And even in the first ones?: that is, in the first two cases, asked in astonishment: but there is definite knowledge at the other entry!
gershom:a2.1: Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda exempts in all of them in the name of Rabbi Shimon. And even in the first case?: with a single entry, why [exempt]? Whichever way you look at it, there is definite knowledge of impurity when he entered.
rashi:a2.2: He forgot that he had walked on the first: although it is a definite impurity, there is nonetheless only partial knowledge, since he forgot the first. It is about this that these two tanna’im disagree in their account of Rabbi Shimon. The first tanna, reporting Rabbi Shimon, exempted only in the last case. In the first cases, since whichever way you look at it there is impurity, there is definite knowledge that he walked on both; even though he forgot that he had walked on the first, partial knowledge is still like knowledge, and it counts as knowledge at the outset. But in the last case there is no definite knowledge.
gershom:a3.1: Rabba [so Rabbeinu Gershom’s text; the daf reads Rava] said: What are we dealing with here? Where he walked on the first, and when he walked on the second he forgot that he had walked on the first, and afterward entered the Temple. Here there is partial knowledge and not all of it: when he walked on the first he did not know he was definitely impure, and when he then walked on the second and had forgotten that he walked on the first, he did not know he was definitely impure.
rashi:a2.3: And Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda holds [Rashi’s heading names Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda where the daf has “Rabbi Shimon”]: although it is a definite impurity, since there is only partial knowledge, it is as though there were none.
gershom:a4.1: The first tanna holds that partial knowledge is like full knowledge, and he is liable; and Rabbi Shimon holds that we do not say partial knowledge is like full knowledge, and he is exempt.
gershom:a5.1: The Master said: He walked etc. And why is he liable? There was no definite knowledge.
rashi:a4.1: Rabbi Yishmael etc.: in the second chapter of Shevuot (14b).
gershom:a6.1: Reish Lakish said: Whose view is this? It is Rabbi Yishmael’s, who says in the first chapter of Shevuot that knowledge at the outset is not required. Therefore even if there was no knowledge at all, he is liable.
gershom:a7.1: And Rabbi Yoḥanan said: You may even say it is the Rabbis’ view, who require knowledge at the beginning and at the end; [nevertheless] he is liable, for he holds that here, regarding impurity, they made knowledge of uncertainty like definite knowledge. Therefore he is liable.
gershom:a8.1: It enters your mind: “here they made it so,” and the same is true for the entire Torah. If so, Rabbi Yoḥanan against Rabbi Yoḥanan is difficult, and Reish Lakish against Reish Lakish is difficult. Rabbi Yoḥanan against Rabbi Yoḥanan: here Rabbi Yoḥanan says that knowledge of uncertainty is like definite knowledge, while there, regarding uncertain forbidden fat, [he said] that knowledge of uncertainty is not like definite knowledge, so that he is not obligated in a sin offering as for definite knowledge, but [only] in a guilt offering as for uncertain knowledge.
rashi:a6.1: And Reish Lakish against Reish Lakish is difficult: for why did he not establish it according to Rabbi [Yehuda HaNasi], and say that knowledge of uncertainty is like definite knowledge?
gershom:a9.1: And Reish Lakish against Reish Lakish is difficult: since Reish Lakish said that Rabbi holds that knowledge of uncertainty divides [transgressions] for sin offerings, why does he establish this case of the paths, where he is liable, according to Rabbi Yishmael? Let him establish it according to Rabbi.
gershom:a10.1: Granted, Rabbi Yoḥanan against Rabbi Yoḥanan is not difficult: it is here, regarding sacred matters, that they made uncertain knowledge at the outset like definite knowledge. For knowledge at the outset regarding sacred food and the Temple we do not find written explicitly; it comes only by inference, as it says: “and it was concealed” implies that he had known. Therefore, since knowledge is not written explicitly, even knowledge of uncertainty suffices and he is liable. But in the rest of the Torah, where knowledge is written explicitly, “or if [his sin] be known to him,” we require: if he has definite knowledge he is liable, and if not, not.
rashi:a8.1: “And it was concealed from him, and he is impure”: this implies that even though there is some concealment regarding the impurity, he is liable.
tosafot:a9.1: Instead of establishing it according to Rabbi Yishmael, let him establish it according to Rabbi: we must say that this does not mean exactly according to Rabbi, for if so, even without the contradiction of Reish Lakish against Reish Lakish, the Gemara could have challenged: let him establish it according to Rabbi on the basis of “knowledge from his teacher’s house” [yedi’at beit rabbo], and that is why he is liable, since it counts as knowledge from his teacher’s house, and Rabbi holds that this is called knowledge. Rather, this is the challenge: instead of establishing it according to Rabbi Yishmael, as a case with no knowledge at all, let him establish it according to Rabbi, as a case of partial knowledge, like knowledge of uncertainty, which Rabbi holds is called knowledge.
gershom:a11.1: But according to Reish Lakish it is difficult: instead of establishing this according to Rabbi Yishmael, let him establish it according to Rabbi.
gershom:a12.1: Indeed, he could have established it according to Rabbi.
tosafot:a10.1: But it is a mishna, as we learned etc.: Rabbi Shmuel of Verdun asked: how is it proven from the mishna cited here that Rabbi Yishmael does not require knowledge at the outset? I could say that he does require it. If it is because he takes “and it was concealed… and it was concealed” for another exposition, we see that Rabbi, who holds that knowledge from his teacher’s house is called knowledge, requires knowledge from his teacher’s house even though he takes “and it was concealed… and it was concealed” for concealment of impurity and concealment of the Temple, as here; and he nevertheless requires knowledge from his teacher’s house from the sense of “and it was concealed,” which implies that he had already known. One can answer: granted that for Rabbi we find elsewhere that he requires knowledge from his teacher’s house, so for the Temple and impurity he requires it too; but for Rabbi Yishmael we do not find anywhere that he requires knowledge from his teacher’s house. One can further answer: if so, it should have said explicitly: “and it was concealed” implies that he had already known.
gershom:a13.1: Rather, this teaches us that Rabbi Yishmael does not require knowledge at the outset. And what does it teach us? It is a mishna in Shevuot that Rabbi Yishmael does not require knowledge at the outset.
rashi:a10.1: “And it was concealed” etc.: since he takes these two [occurrences of] “and it was concealed” for this exposition, evidently he does not hold that knowledge is required at the outset. For the knowledge of impurity that is required at the beginning and at the end is derived only from these two [occurrences of] “and it was concealed,” as we said in the first chapter of Shevuot (4a).
gershom:a14.1: For we learned: “and it was concealed from him” twice, one to make him liable for concealment of impurity and one to make him liable for concealment of the Temple and its sacred food. For whoever requires knowledge at the outset derives it from “and it was concealed from him,” which is written twice, as was said above: “and it was concealed,” [so] he had known, “and it was concealed.”
gershom:a15.1: It was necessary to teach us: lest you say that although Rabbi Yishmael does not derive knowledge at the outset from the verses, as we said, since he takes them for concealment of the Temple and of impurity, he does hold it from tradition, from reasoning. Reish Lakish teaches us that he does not.
rashi:a12.1: Mishna. Forbidden fat and notar before him: and he thought both of them were permitted fat.
rashi:a12.2: His menstruating wife and his sister with him in the house: he had intercourse with one of them, thinking she was his wife and thinking she was pure, and it turned out that his wife was menstruating; and moreover it is uncertain with which of them he had intercourse.
gershom:a16.1: Shabbat and Yom Kippur: for example, Yom Kippur fell on Sunday, and he performed labor at twilight at the end of Shabbat. Or [the dispute is] about one who performs labor and does not know of which primary category of labor he performed, or of which subcategory of a primary labor.
rashi:a12.3: And Rabbi Yehoshua exempts: this is explained in the Gemara: “wherein he has sinned,” until it becomes known to him with what he sinned.
rashi:a14.1: Or one who performs: labor on Shabbat and does not know which labor he performed, whether plowing or sowing.
rashi:a14.2: Even from a provisional guilt offering: this is explained in the Gemara.
rashi:a15.1: They did not disagree: Rabbi Eliezer, who says we do not require that he know with what he sinned, [and Rabbi Yehoshua, who says we require that he know with what he sinned].
rashi:a15.2: Regarding a matter from one category: for example, two trees of one species were before him, and he does not know whether he picked from this one or from that one.
rashi:a15.3: That he is liable: for he knew with what he sinned, which labor he performed: that he sinned by picking figs.
gershom:b16.1: Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua did not disagree about a matter from one category, that he is liable: for example, two vines or two fig trees were before him, and he intended to pick from this one and picked from the other. He is liable, since it is one category: vine and vine, or fig tree and fig tree.
rashi:a15.4: Over what did they disagree? Over a matter from two categories: for example, it is uncertain whether he reaped or ground; or uncertain whether figs or grapes; and likewise where he intended this and did that. The word “bah” [“wherein”] written in the verse refers both to the knowledge and to the sin. According to Rabbi Yehoshua, [he is not liable] until he intends to sin with it, and at the time of knowledge he knows with what he sinned. According to Rabbi Eliezer, since he intended a matter that involves a sin, and at the time of knowledge it became known to him that he sinned, that suffices.
gershom:b17.1: Over what did they disagree? Over a matter from two categories: for example, he intended to harvest grapes and reaped, or to harvest grapes and picked figs. Rabbi Eliezer deems him liable and Rabbi Yehoshua exempts.
gershom:b18.1: Rabbi Yehuda says: not only in a matter from one category does Rabbi Eliezer deem him liable, but even [where he intended] to pick figs and picked grapes etc., which is a matter from two categories, even so Rabbi Eliezer deems him liable and Rabbi Yehoshua exempts. And I wonder if Rabbi Yehoshua would exempt in this, for either way he performed a labor.
rashi:a16.1: And I wonder if he exempted in it: that is, on what grounds would Rabbi Yehoshua exempt in this case? He intended a forbidden act.
rashi:a16.2: If so: if one who acts unawares in this way is liable, why is “bah” stated?
rashi:a16.3: To exclude one who acts unawares: with a permitted act, for example, [he intended] to cut something detached and he cut something attached. But this one, who acts unawares with a forbidden act, is liable.
gershom:b19.1: Rabbi Shimon Shezuri said to him [a note in the printed text: from our master’s words it appears that he read in the mishna, “Rabbi Shimon Shezuri said to him: If so, why is it stated” etc., and that Rabbi Yehuda answered him, “to exclude one who acts unawares”]: Yes, he is certainly exempt in this, for it is not as you say. Why is “wherein he has sinned” stated? It implies: until he sinned in it, in the very labor he intended, and this one did one he did not intend. Rabbi Yehuda said to him: That “wherein he has sinned” comes to exclude one who acts unawares with a permitted act and ends up with a prohibited one, according to Rava as he holds and according to Abaye as he holds. But [regarding one who acts unawares with a prohibited act], I wonder if Rabbi Yehoshua would exempt in it.
gershom:a17.1: Whichever way you look at it etc.: this is Rabbi Eliezer’s reason for imposing a sin offering: whichever way you look at it.
gershom:a18.1: And Rabbi Yehoshua exempts: because it is written “wherein he has sinned,” until it becomes known with what he sinned.
rashi:a18.1: Gemara. He requires it to exclude one who acts unawares: for example, he intended this one and did another. And if you ask: if so, if Rabbi Eliezer holds like Rav Naḥman, then this “bah” that Rabbi Eliezer expounds to exclude one who acts unawares is unnecessary, since he could learn it from “planned labor,” which Rav Naḥman cites. It seems to me that Rabbi Eliezer does not hold like Rav Naḥman, who expounds “the Torah prohibited planned labor,” since that exposition does not seem [persuasive] to him; and the Gemara cites Rav Naḥman only because he says explicitly that one who acts unawares on Shabbat is exempt. But Rabbi Yehoshua, who expounds “wherein he has sinned” as “until it becomes known to him with what he sinned,” expounds like Rav Naḥman: the Torah prohibited planned labor.
gershom:a19.1: To exclude one who acts unawares: one who is occupied with them for the sake of something else and comes to a prohibition without intent.
rashi:b1.1: One who acts unawares with fats: for example, permitted fat and forbidden fat were before him, and it was known that this is forbidden fat and this is permitted fat. He intended to eat the permitted fat, looked elsewhere, and his hand went to the forbidden fat and he ate it. Alternatively, [two pieces of] forbidden fat were before him and he thought it was permitted fat, and he intended to eat this piece and ate that one. This is not like an unwitting sinner [shogeg], for an unwitting sinner is one who intended this very piece but thought it was permitted fat.
rashi:b1.2: One who acts unawares with forbidden relations: for example, he intended to have intercourse with his wife, who was menstruating, and thought she was pure; his sister and his wife were before him, and his wife slipped away without his knowing, and his sister came in her place. This is not like an unwitting sinner, for an unwitting sinner is one who intended this very woman but thought she was his wife.
gershom:b1.1: [A printer’s note marks that the preceding comments belong to the previous amud.] One who acts unawares, in what? If with fats and forbidden relations: with fats, for example, he thought it was saliva and swallowed it, and it was forbidden fat; with forbidden relations, for example, he fell from a roof and [unintentionally] came into intercourse [with a forbidden woman]. Such a one is liable, for he derived pleasure. Rather, [the verse comes] to exclude one who acts unawares on Shabbat with a permitted act and comes to a prohibition without knowing it, who is exempt, for the Torah prohibited planned labor: all the labors we derive from the Tabernacle, and of the Tabernacle “planned labor” [melekhet maḥashevet] is written. [It excludes] one who is occupied with something else. And what is the case of one acting unawares on Shabbat who is exempt? According to Rava and Abaye, who disagree in Tractate Shabbat.
rashi:b2.1: Rather, one who acts unawares on Shabbat: the verse comes to exempt him for this. One who acts unawares on Shabbat is explained below.
rashi:b2.2: Planned labor: that he planned and intended this very labor.
rashi:b3.1: You find it: one who acts unawares on Shabbat, for example, where he intended etc.
gershom:b2.1: According to Rava: for example, he intended to cut some detached food and cut something attached, so that his intention was not carried out.
rashi:b3.2: To lift: he is exempt according to all, for this is one who acts unawares, since he did not intend any cutting.
tosafot:b4.1: As it was stated: he intended to lift the detached and cut the attached: according to what we have explained, one must say that what came into his hand, attached, was the very plant he intended. For if he cut a different attached plant, why mention that he intended [to lift] something detached? Even if he had intended an attached plant he would be exempt, as in the case of two lamps where he intended to extinguish this one and extinguished that one. Rabbeinu Shlomo Yitzḥaki [Rashi] did not explain it this way.
tosafot:b4.2: For he did not intend a prohibited cutting: and if you say, an unwitting sinner anywhere in the Torah also does not intend a prohibition! One can say: anywhere in the Torah, when he says it is permitted, he is unwitting about a matter that is known to us to be prohibited; but here he intends something that is permitted according to everyone, had it been as he thought. That is why he is exempt: he is one who acts unawares.
rashi:b5.1: You were diligent after me: that is, you have defeated me and bested me.
gershom:b3.1: It is taught in a baraita: Rabbi Yosei said to the Sages: You were diligent after me and answered me with a winning answer.
rashi:b6.1: He lifted: an object at twilight between Shabbat and Yom Kippur in order to carry it out, where he is liable immediately for the lifting, since there is a lifting that is [itself] a carrying out; for example, where the object is adjacent to the public domain and he is standing in the public domain. What is the halakha? How can you say there: part of it today and part of it tomorrow?
rashi:b6.2: You were diligent after me: and you thought to defeat me, but you accomplished nothing, for one can also say: part of the lifting today and part of the lifting tomorrow.
gershom:b4.1: This is what they said to him, and this is how they answered your words [Rabbi Yosei], for you say he performed part of the labor today and part tomorrow and is exempt, since he did not perform a complete labor in one day: If he lifted at twilight, what is the halakha? For example, he was standing in a private domain at twilight and lifted an object in the public domain. From the moment he lifts it he is liable, according to the reasoning of the one who holds that the uprooting need not be for the sake of placing; rather, once he has lifted it, it is a complete primary labor. And lifting can take place in the blink of an eye, so one cannot say part of it was today and part tomorrow. Therefore he said to them: You were diligent after me and answered me. Some say: lifting at twilight [refers to] one who strikes with a hammer on the anvil; it is about that lifting that they answered him, for it is among the primary labors and takes no time.
gershom:b5.1: And let him say to them: that lifting too was partly today, for example, the lifting was today and the striking on the anvil tomorrow; for Rabbi Yosei holds that twilight lasts the blink of an eye.
gershom:b6.1: That is also what he is saying to them: and “you were diligent after me” means that there is nothing in your words.
rashi:b8.1: And according to Rabbi Yosei: granted that it is part today and part tomorrow, [still,] it is the completion of a labor. Why does he say that according to all he is exempt? We have heard that Rabbi Eliezer deems liable [for completing a labor].
gershom:b7.1: And according to Rabbi Yosei, for the completion of a labor, according to Rabbi Eliezer [would he be exempt]? But we have heard that he is liable, for he says “or one on the woven fabric, he is liable,” which is the completion of a labor. So here too, with the lifting at twilight, let him be liable for the completion of the labor, for the completion of the labor was on one day. So why did Rabbi Yosei exempt?
rashi:b9.1: And two on the woven fabric: this is the whole measure. At the beginning, the reason he requires three is that [two] come apart, since two do not hold. But here one can say: half of it today and half of it tomorrow.
gershom:b8.1: Rav Yosef said: Rabbi Yosei, according to Rabbi Eliezer, teaches it thus: Rabbi Eliezer says, “or two on the woven fabric, he is liable,” for the completion of a labor [must] be the measure of a complete labor, as the reason is given in Tractate Shabbat: one thread comes apart, two do not. And since the completion of the labor requires the measure of a complete labor, he exempts, for I say he did part today and part tomorrow.
rashi:b10.1: “If anyone sin… though he does not know it, yet is he guilty”: this is written regarding the provisional guilt offering.
gershom:b9.1: “If anyone sin… though he does not know it”: whether he sinned or not, for example, uncertain whether forbidden fat or permitted fat.
gershom:b10.1: To exclude this one, who knew that he sinned: definitely, but does not know of which type of labor.
gershom:b11.1: Rabbi Shimon said to him: On the contrary, this is the very one who brings a provisional guilt offering, as it is stated: “and do… though he does not know it”: he certainly did it but did not know what he did, and he brings his guilt offering.
gershom:b12.1: But uncertain whether he ate forbidden fat, uncertain whether he did not eat: that he brings a provisional guilt offering, which seems obvious to you, is not obvious. Rather, go and ask whether he brings a provisional guilt offering or not, for he did not know that he certainly did it.
rashi:b11.1: What was concluded about it: about “uncertain whether he ate, uncertain whether he did not eat,” according to Rabbi Shimon.
gershom:b13.1: What was concluded about it: about what he said, “go and ask about it,” in the case of uncertain whether he ate or did not eat: what does Rabbi Shimon hold about it?
rashi:b12.1: He sinned and does not know with what he sinned: for example, forbidden fat and notar were before him and he does not know which of them he ate. Or uncertain whether he sinned, uncertain whether he did not sin: for example, permitted fat and forbidden fat were before him.
gershom:b14.1: Come and hear, as it is taught: he sinned and does not know what he sinned, [that is,] in which type of labor; or uncertain whether he sinned, uncertain whether he did not sin, which is uncertain whether he ate, uncertain whether he did not eat: he brings a provisional guilt offering.
gershom:b15.1: Whom did you hear who says: “he sinned” etc.
rashi:b15.1: The babies are one who acts unawares: for he intended to circumcise this one and circumcised that one. [This is unlike] an unwitting sinner, as where he intended this very one but thought he had been born on Shabbat.
rashi:b16.1: In a matter that is not a mitzva: for example, he intended this fig and picked that one.
gershom:b20.1: Rabbi Yehoshua exempted only because he holds that [one who] erred in a matter of a mitzva, thinking he is [performing] a mitzva, as here, where he thought its mitzva was today and it is not until tomorrow, is exempt since he erred in a matter of a mitzva. But one who acts unawares in a matter that is not a mitzva and comes to a prohibition on Shabbat, even Rabbi Yehoshua deems liable. This is a refutation of Shmuel, who said that one who acts unawares on Shabbat is exempt according to all.
rashi:b17.1: One who is destructive with a wound is liable: for so we say in Bava Kamma, in the chapter HaMani’aḥ et HaKad (34b): all who are destructive are exempt, except for one who wounds and one who kindles.
gershom:b21.1: He said to him: from here you cannot infer. For here, what is the reason Rabbi Eliezer deems liable in the case of the babies? Since one who is destructive with a wound on Shabbat is generally liable according to all, here too, with circumcision, one who acts unawares with a wound that is not a mitzva is also liable. But in all other matters of Shabbat, one who acts unawares is exempt according to all.
rashi:b19.1: But within one type even Rabbi Yehoshua deems liable: yet you said that one who acts unawares on Shabbat is exempt, which implies without qualification, even within one type.
rashi:b19.2: Even Rabbi Yehoshua deems liable: for he is not one who acts unawares, since he intended to pick figs and picked figs. Although Abaye and Rava exempt one who acts unawares only where he intended a permitted act, for example, to cut something detached, Shmuel exempts even one who acts unawares with a prohibited act, since the Gemara phrased his statement as “the Torah prohibited planned labor,” implying that he must intend it.
tosafot:b19.1: But within one type even Rabbi Yehoshua deems liable: that is why the Gemara raises the objection against Shmuel and not against Abaye and Rava above. According to Shmuel, the case is this one, of one who intends a prohibited act and is exempt on account of “planned labor.” But it does not object against Abaye and Rava, since they do not speak of this; they speak of one who intended a permitted act, who is exempt on account of “bah,” to exclude one who acts unawares, for that is the discussion above.
gershom:b22.1: But here, it is one acting unawares on Shabbat with this species who picked another species, and Rabbi Eliezer deems him liable; and even Rabbi Yehoshua exempted only from species to species, when he was occupied with one species and ended up with another. But within one species, for example, he was occupied with this vine and picked another, even Rabbi Yehoshua deems liable, for he did the type of labor he intended. Evidently one who acts unawares on Shabbat is liable.
rashi:b20.1: And follow after me: explain [the mishna] as I do, that one who acts unawares is exempt; and here he is not one who acts unawares, for the one he intended is the one he picked. And why does Rabbi Yehoshua exempt? Where the picker lost his train of thought: his initial thought of the picking was lost from his mind and he forgot it. For example, he intended to pick grapes, forgot, and thought, “I want figs,” and his hand went onto the grapes and picked them without intent. His desire was fulfilled, for he needed grapes, [but his thought was not fulfilled,] for at the time of picking he thought of figs, so it turns out that his thought was not fulfilled. And we require both, his desire and his thought.
tosafot:b20.1: What are we dealing with here? Where the picker lost his train of thought, for example, he intended etc.: and about this Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua disagree, as the Gemara explains. Now it is well that the Gemara does not object, “but within one type he is liable,” for the parallel case within one type is what it speaks of: for example, he intended to pick these figs, forgot and thought he wanted other figs on another side, and his hand went onto the first figs. That is why he is liable, since at first he intended these figs. For the ruling that he is exempt on account of “planned labor,” where he intended to cut this attached plant and cut another attached plant, speaks of where the picker did not lose his train of thought, for he never intended anything but that first attached plant.
gershom:b23.1: Shmuel said to him: What are we dealing with here, where Rabbi Eliezer deems liable? Where the picker lost his train of thought: that is, what he first intended to pick was lost and forgotten from his mind. For example, he first intended to pick grapes, forgot, and thought he wanted to pick figs; and when he sought to pick figs, his hand went without his knowledge onto the grapes and picked them.
gershom:b24.1: For Rabbi Eliezer holds: his intention was carried out: what he first intended, and he is liable.
gershom:b25.1: And Rabbi Yehoshua holds: his desire and his thought were not carried out: at the time he picked, his desire and his thought were not carried out, for he sought figs and picked grapes. But in general, even within one species, where he did not pick the very one he thought of but one from another vine, he is exempt according to all; and all the more so with two species.
